La résilience d’une féministe tamoule: The Resilience of a Tamil Feminist
Entre sa famille et son travail d’interv: Between her family and her work as a community worker, she takes things with positivity and optimism.
Sivambikai « Ambika » Sivamoorthy mène a: Sivambikai “Ambika” Sivamoorthy now leads a fulfilling life in Montréal.
Entre sa famille et son travail d’interv: Between her family and her work as a community worker, she takes things with positivity and optimism. These two great qualities have allowed her to get through hardships that would have broken many others.
De son parcours d’immigration, digne d’u: From her immigration journey, worthy of a thriller, to her community involvement among her own people, she tells us her story.
« Mon périple d’immigration a été diffic: “My immigration journey was difficult,” Ambika recalls. Several decades ago, she was forced to flee Jaffna, her hometown in northern Sri Lanka, where her community, the Tamils, lives. “The civil war between the government and the Tamils was raging at that time,” she explains. Ambika and her compatriots hid in an abandoned bungalow in a palm grove, waiting for a fishing boat to take them to southern India.
Quelques jours plus tard, lors d’une nui: A few days later, on a cold, windy night, she boarded, dressed in dark clothes so the coast guard wouldn’t spot her. When she arrived in India, she was welcomed by good Samaritans who took her in. She would stay there for three years. When stability returned to Sri Lanka, Ambika went back to her country.
De retour chez elle, la jeune femme se t: Back home, the young woman found a job at a call centre in the capital, Colombo. The peace was short-lived. A colleague was accused of carrying out a bombing, and the police burst into her workplace. Ambika was violently interrogated. “The police wanted me to help them identify suspects. They were very rough and didn’t treat me well because I wasn’t comfortable with the majority language, Sinhala. They thought I was pretending not to understand,” she says indignantly. She narrowly escaped arrest.
L’incident pousse la mère d’Ambika à tou: The incident led Ambika’s mother to do everything she could to protect her daughter from an arbitrary arrest, which would expose her to the risk of the sexual violence committed against women who end up in the justice system. She wanted her daughter to immigrate to Canada. So, with her old passport, Ambika travelled to Singapore, where her family paid migrant smugglers $7,000 to get her to Canada. They took her to Malaysia to wait for false papers.
« En route pour la Malaisie, on a dû se: “On the way to Malaysia, we had to hide in a small compartment under the bus to escape the authorities. There were five or six of us crammed in there!” she recalls. After an interminable wait of several months, Ambika received a fake Malaysian passport. “On the day I left, I put on jeans for the first time in my life so I would look Canadian,” says Ambika. The smuggler taught her what to say and how to answer the immigration officers’ questions. “They also put me in a wheelchair with a fake bandage on my foot. I pretended I’d had an accident and needed to return to Canada,” she says. In 1994, Ambika landed in Canada late at night.
Comme il est trop tard pour trouver un i: Since it was too late to find an interpreter, she got through customs successfully. Of course, she didn’t say that she spoke English. Ambika then applied for refugee status, which was granted the following year.
<strong>« Mon père était féministe avec: “My father was a feminist with his daughters. He wanted us to be independent”
Ambika se rend d’abord chez sa tante et: Ambika first went to stay with her aunt and uncle in Hamilton, Ontario. Finding her uncle’s sexist behaviour hard to bear, she left to make it on her own. “When I arrived, my aunt had already been living in Canada for 30 years. She was still a typical Sri Lankan woman and wanted me to be like her,” Ambika exclaims. She remembers her uncle, who tried to control everything and gave her orders, unlike what she had known at home.
« Mon père était féministe avec ses fill: “My father was a feminist with his daughters. He wanted us to be independent and to take care of our own affairs,” says Ambika. In a culture where it can be frowned upon for women to go out, to come home after 6 p.m. and to talk with men, Ambika’s father saw no problem with any of it.
Quand sa fille s’est retrouvée seule dan: When his daughter found herself alone in another country, forced to be strong and independent, she was able to appreciate just how precious the feminist values passed on to her were.
<strong>Une communauté soudée de femmes: A close-knit community of South Asian women
Après un court séjour à Toronto, Ambika: After a short stay in Toronto, Ambika arrived in Montréal alone in 1996. “I came to visit a friend who lived in Montréal, and I loved the city right away,” she says of the metropolis, which reminded her of her hometown. Her husband, who had stayed in Sri Lanka, joined her three years later, after a long bureaucratic battle with Canadian immigration.
Aujourd’hui, Ambika est une femme heureu: Today, Ambika is a happy woman. At 62, she works at the South Asian Women’s Community Centre in Montréal, where she helps women build their lives in Quebec. She regularly lends a hand with filling out administrative forms and supports them in situations of domestic violence.
« J’adore mon travail. Je suis tellement: “I love my job. I’m so happy to be able to help people, whether they’re Sinhalese or Tamil, it doesn’t matter to me,” says Ambika, herself a Tamil who lived through the war. “The Sinhalese appreciate me enormously and come to me when they need help,” says the sixty-something. Her work has allowed her to find a community of women like her and to put her own life in perspective. “I’m so grateful to God for giving me this job.
J’y rencontre beaucoup de gens qui viven: I meet so many people there who are going through difficult situations, who don’t speak French or English, who are alone in a new country. My own problems now seem tiny!” says the woman who, nonetheless, has had to go through great hardships.
